core.text: Deponents build their participle like everyone else, but it means the opposite: **the perfect participle of a deponent verb (active meaning: locutus = having spoken)**. *Haec locūta, Ariadna …* — having said this, Ariadne …; *fīlum secūtus* — having followed the thread. This is the only 'having done' participle Latin has, so writers use it constantly to tell what someone did just before the main verb. Latin name: *participium perfecti verbi deponentis*.
English says *having spoken*, *having set out* — a participle for an action the same person finished first.
Participle stem + -us -a -um, agreeing with the person who did the action; translate 'having …-ed'.

invented.en: The boy, having slipped from the bed, cries.

core.text: *Locūtus* and *laudātus* look identical, but **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudatus = praised)** of an ordinary verb is passive. Check the dictionary form: a verb whose infinitive ends in -ī / -ārī / -ērī / -īrī is deponent, and its participle is active — *profecta* is 'having set out', not 'having been set out'.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 22) set out the gap: ordinary verbs have a present active and a perfect passive participle only; deponents have present active (*loquēns*) and perfect active (*locūtus*). Their examples: *puer lāpsus* (the boy having slipped), *fēmina profecta*, *canēs secūtī*, *virōs operātōs*.
